title: Faraday cage
description: Enclosure of conductive mesh used to block electric fields
wiki_lead:
A Faraday cage or Faraday shield is an enclosure used to block some electromagnetic fields. A Faraday shield may be formed by a continuous covering of conductive material, or in the case of a Faraday cage, by a mesh of such materials. Faraday cages are named after the scientist Michael Faraday, who first constructed one in 1836.
Faraday cages work because an external electrical field will cause the electric charges within the cage's conducting material to be distributed in a way that cancels out the field's effect inside the cage. This phenomenon can be used to protect sensitive electronic equipment (for example RF receivers) from external radio frequency interference (RFI), often during testing or alignment of the device. Faraday cages are also used to protect people and equipment against electric currents such as lightning strikes and electrostatic discharges, because the cage conducts electrical current around the outside of the enclosed space and none passes through to the interior.
Faraday cages cannot block stable or slowly varying magnetic fields, such as the Earth's magnetic field (a compass will still work inside one). To a large degree, however, they shield the interior from external electromagnetic radiation if the conductor is thick enough and any hole is significantly smaller than the wavelength of the radiation. For example, certain computer forensic electronic systems test procedures that require an electromagnetic interference free environment can be carried out within a screened room. These rooms are spaces that are completely enclosed by one or more layers of a fine metal mesh or perforated sheet metal. The metal layers are grounded to dissipate any electric currents generated from external or internal electromagnetic fields, and thus they block a large amount of the electromagnetic interference (see also electromagnetic shielding). They provide less attenuation of outgoing transmissions than incoming: they can block electromagnetic pulse (EMP) waves from natural phenomena very effectively, but especially in upper frequencies, a tracking device may be able to penetrate from within the cage (e.g., some cell phones operate at various radio frequencies, so while one frequency may not work, another one will).
The reception or transmission of radio waves, a form of electromagnetic radiation, to or from an antenna within a Faraday cage is heavily attenuated or blocked by the cage; however, a Faraday cage has varied attenuation depending on wave form, frequency, or the distance from receiver or transmitter, and receiver or transmitter power. Near-field, high-powered frequency transmissions like HF RFID are more likely to penetrate. Solid cages generally attenuate fields over a broader frequency range than mesh cages.

grok_lead: A Faraday cage is an enclosure formed by conductive material, such as metal sheets or mesh, that effectively blocks external electric fields and electromagnetic radiation by redistributing charges on its surface to create a region of zero net field inside. Named after British physicist Michael Faraday, who constructed the first one in 1836, the device demonstrates a fundamental principle of electrostatics: charges reside only on the outer surface of a conductor, leaving the interior shielded from external influences. In Faraday's seminal experiment, he lined a room with metal foil and subjected it to high-voltage electrostatic discharges from a generator; an electroscope placed inside registered no charge, confirming that the electric field did not penetrate the enclosure. The operating principle relies on electrostatic induction, where free electrons in the conductive material rapidly rearrange to oppose and cancel incoming electric fields, ensuring the interior remains at an equipotential with no net field. For electromagnetic waves, such as radio frequencies, the cage attenuates signals if the openings (in mesh designs) are smaller than the wavelength of the radiation, preventing propagation while allowing induced currents to dissipate energy on the surface. Grounding the cage enhances performance by providing a path for excess charges, though it is not strictly necessary for basic shielding. This effect extends to time-varying magnetic fields through eddy currents that generate opposing fields, though shielding of static or low-frequency magnetic fields requires specialized high-permeability materials like mu-metal. Faraday cages find widespread applications in protecting sensitive electronics from interference, such as in electrochemical laboratories where they reduce noise in measurements like voltammetry and impedance spectroscopy. In aviation, they safeguard aircraft structuresâoften using copper mesh embedded in compositesâagainst lightning strikes by directing currents around the fuselage, minimizing damage to critical systems and protecting thousands of flights annually. Other uses include shielding microwave ovens, securing data centers from radiofrequency attacks, and enclosing vehicles like cars, which naturally act as cages during electrical storms.
